title: Flaki, Krupnik and Liver
lead: Masovian cuisine is a mix of rural and Warsaw traditions. Find out what is worth eating in Warsaw and Masovia. Slow travel through Masovian cuisine.
body:
Why Masovian cuisine, differently

Masovian cuisine is the cuisine of a region where rural and urban traditions meet. On one hand, simple rural dishes — krupnik, groats, potatoes — on the other, refined Warsaw cuisine — flaki, liver, duck. All this makes one of the more interesting regional cuisines in Poland. Masovia is a region of central Poland, around Warsaw, where for centuries peasants, burghers, nobility, and Jews lived side by side — and each of these cultures brought something to the local cuisine.

Slow travel through Masovian cuisine is a celebration of taste and tradition. Instead of rushing from restaurant to restaurant, stop in one longer — in a village inn, in a milk bar, in a restaurant in Warsaw. Each dish has its own story, its own cook, its own town or village. Ask where the ingredients come from, how the dish is prepared, who passed down the recipe. This is a journey that rewards those who slow down — the longer you are in one place, the more flavors you can truly get to know.

What to see

Masovian cuisine splits into several categories: meat dishes (Warsaw flaki, poultry liver, Masovian duck), fish dishes (Jewish-style carp), soups (Masovian krupnik, żur), flour dishes (pierogi, dumplings, racuchy), baked goods (Masovian bread, cheesecake). Exploring the culinary region of Masovia takes 2–3 days.

Meat dishes

  • Warsaw flaki — a classic of Warsaw cuisine. Beef tripe soup with vegetables, marjoram, and paprika. Served with a bread roll or bread. A labor-intensive dish, but deeply rooted in the capital's tradition.
  • Poultry liver — fried poultry liver with onion and apple. Served with potatoes and salad. A classic of Warsaw cuisine.
  • Masovian duck — roast duck with apples, marjoram, and caraway. Served with modra kapusta and dumplings. In the Masovian version — with dried plums and honey.
  • Jewish-style carp — a traditional Warsaw dish, derived from Jewish cuisine. Carp in jelly with raisins, almonds, and spices. Served at Christmas Eve and holidays.

Soups and flour dishes

  • Masovian krupnik — barley groat soup with vegetables and meat. In the Masovian version — with dried mushrooms and sour cream. Hearty, warming.
  • Masovian żur — sour rye soup with white sausage and egg. A Masovian classic.
  • Pierogi with cabbage and mushrooms — traditional pierogi, which in Masovia have their own specificity — the filling is sweeter, with dried plums and onion. Served at Christmas Eve, weddings, and family celebrations.
  • Masovian dumplings — dumplings made of flour and water, served with mushroom or meat sauce. A simple, filling dish.
  • Apple racuchy — yeast pancakes with apples, fried in a pan. Popular in Masovia as a dessert or afternoon tea.

Baked goods and other specialties

  • Masovian bread — sourdough bread made from rye and wheat flour. Characteristic of Masovian villages, still baked in home ovens.
  • Masovian cheesecake — cheesecake with curd cheese, raisins, and orange peel. Available at pastry shops in Warsaw.
  • Masovian makowiec — yeast cake with poppy seeds, dried fruit, and icing. Served at holidays and family celebrations.
  • Beer from local breweries — several craft breweries in the region (Browar Waszczukowe, Browar Maryensztadt).
  • Masovian liqueurs — krupnik, herbal liqueurs, available in shops with local products.

When to go

  • April–June — the best time for slow travel. Fewer tourists, fresh seasonal produce, long days. Worth a walk through markets.
  • July–September — season for fresh vegetables, fruit, mushrooms. Worth it for markets and culinary festivals.
  • September–October — season for mushrooms, pumpkins, plums. September and October are good times for mushroom picking in Masovian forests.
  • November–March — season for bigos, flaki, żur. Worth it for winter cuisine, especially during the holiday season.

Getting there

Masovian cuisine is from the central region of Poland — best to travel by car or train, connecting several towns in one trip.

  • By train: Warsaw, Płock, Radom, Siedlce have railway stations, with connections from most Polish cities.
  • By car: ~3 hours from Kraków (S7), ~4 hours from Gdańsk (S7), ~3 hours from Poznań (S8 and A2).
  • By bus: PKS and private operators serve most towns on the route.

How much time you need

A weekend (2 days) is the minimum — Warsaw (milk bars, flaki, liver) and surroundings.

Three days is realistic for a first visit. Warsaw, Płock, Pułtusk, Żelazowa Wola.

A week lets you explore the whole culinary region of Masovia — all the most important dishes and places.

What to eat and where to sleep

Instead of restaurants, choose milk bars and village inns. There, cooks prepare what they have known since childhood, and they do it best.

  • Warsaw flaki — a Warsaw classic, available at milk bars and restaurants.
  • Poultry liver — a Warsaw classic, available at milk bars and restaurants.
  • Masovian duck — a Masovian classic, available in elegant restaurants.
  • Jewish-style carp — a traditional Warsaw dish, available in Jewish restaurants.
  • Apple racuchy — a popular Masovian dessert, available at milk bars.
  • Beer from local breweries — several craft breweries in the region.

Accommodation: Warsaw (largest choice, more options), Płock (town, more options), Radom (town, more options), Siedlce (town, more options), agritourism farms in villages (quiet, home-cooked food).

Practical tips

  • Milk bars — usually open from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., often closed on weekends. Check hours before your trip.
  • Regional restaurants — look for places where cooks prepare traditional recipes. Avoid tourist restaurants in city centres.
  • Culinary workshops — many farms and agritourism businesses offer workshops (making pierogi, baking bread, making flaki). Book ahead.
  • Diet — Masovian cuisine can be heavy and filling. Eat smaller portions to try more dishes.
  • Markets — the best place to buy local products (cheeses, honey, cold cuts, mushrooms).
  • Weather — weather in the region can be changeable. Even in July, bring a rain jacket.
  • Signal — good in towns, weaker in villages. Have an offline map.
tip: Order Warsaw flaki at one of the milk bars in Warsaw — preferably with a bread roll and fresh pepper, as it has been served in the capital for generations.
